# Innovation and Entrepreneurship {#innovation-entrepreneurship}

In 1972 the British music and electronics company EMI unveiled the first
commercial computed tomography (CT) scanner, the work of its engineer Godfrey
Hounsfield, who later shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for
the invention. Within a few years, established medical-equipment makers such as
General Electric had overtaken EMI in the market it had created, and EMI soon
left the business. Two decades later, Apple entered a mobile-phone industry it
had not invented and captured a share of industry profits far larger than its
share of units. Why do some pioneers capture the value of their innovations
while others hand it to imitators? Why do well-managed incumbents so often lose
to entrants with inferior products? And how do founders build ventures when
the market they are aiming at does not yet exist?

This chapter assembles the theories that management scholars use to answer
those questions. The first half concerns **innovation**: how new technologies
replace old ones (**[creative destruction](#creative-destruction)**), why incumbents stumble
(**disruptive** and **[architectural innovation](#architectural-innovation)**), how industries settle on
**dominant designs**, who profits from a new technology (**profiting from
innovation**), and how firms draw on external knowledge (**[open innovation](#open-innovation)**).
The second half concerns **entrepreneurship**: how opportunities arise
(**discovery and creation**), how expert founders reason under uncertainty
(**[effectuation](#effectuation)**), how they build with whatever is at hand (**[bricolage](#bricolage)**), and
why young organizations die at high rates (**[liability of newness](#liability-of-newness)**). The
theories complement those on [Dynamic capabilities](#dynamic-capabilities-framework) (Section \@ref(dynamic-capabilities-framework))
in Chapter 5 and on [Diffusion of innovations](#diffusion-of-innovations) (Section \@ref(diffusion-of-innovations)) in
Chapter 10. Where those chapters ask how firms renew themselves and how
adopters take up new products, this chapter asks where innovations come from,
whom they destroy, and who captures their value (Table \@ref(tab:tab-ie-glance)).

```{r tab-ie-glance}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Theory, ~`Core question`, ~`Level of analysis`, ~`Key source`,
  "[Creative destruction](#creative-destruction)", "How does innovation drive economic change and growth?", "Economy / industry", "Schumpeter (1934, 1942), Aghion & Howitt (1992)",
  "[Disruptive innovation](#disruptive-innovation)", "Why do well-run incumbents lose to inferior entrants?", "Firm / industry", "Bower & Christensen (1995), Christensen (1997)",
  "[Profiting from innovation](#profiting-from-innovation)", "Who captures the value an innovation creates?", "Firm / industry", "Teece (1986)",
  "[Architectural innovation](#architectural-innovation)", "Why do small changes in product architecture defeat incumbents?", "Firm / product", "Henderson & Clark (1990)",
  "[Dominant design and technology cycles](#dominant-design)", "How do industries converge on one design, and what follows?", "Industry / technology", "Abernathy & Utterback (1978), Anderson & Tushman (1990)",
  "[Open innovation](#open-innovation)", "When should firms use external ideas and paths to market?", "Firm", "Chesbrough (2003), Laursen & Salter (2006)",
  "[Effectuation](#effectuation)", "How do expert entrepreneurs decide under uncertainty?", "Individual / venture", "Sarasvathy (2001)",
  "[Opportunity discovery and creation](#opportunity-discovery-creation)", "Do entrepreneurs find opportunities or make them?", "Individual / market", "Shane & Venkataraman (2000), Alvarez & Barney (2007)",
  "[Bricolage](#bricolage)", "How do resource-poor ventures build something from nothing?", "Venture", "Baker & Nelson (2005)",
  "[Liability of newness](#liability-of-newness)", "Why do young organizations fail at higher rates?", "Organization / population", "Stinchcombe (1965), Freeman, Carroll & Hannan (1983)"

## Creative Destruction {#creative-destruction}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Capitalist economies develop through innovation, the carrying
out of new combinations, which creates new products, firms, and industries
while destroying the value of the old ones. Temporary monopoly profits from
innovation are both the reward and the engine of the process.

**Origins.** Economics. @schumpeter1934, first published in German in 1911,
introduced the entrepreneur as the agent of "new combinations".
@schumpeter1942 coined the phrase *creative destruction* and shifted attention
to the research laboratories of large firms. @aghion1992 formalized the idea in
endogenous growth theory.

**Level of analysis.** Economy and industry, with the entrepreneur or innovating
firm as the micro-level agent.

**Key constructs.** New combinations, entrepreneur, innovation rents,
imitation, obsolescence, business stealing, quality ladder.

**Boundary conditions.** Strongest where innovations are rivalrous with existing
products and where rents can be captured for a time. Weaker for innovations that
complement rather than replace existing goods.

**Related theories.** [Dynamic capabilities](#dynamic-capabilities-framework) (Section \@ref(dynamic-capabilities-framework)),
[Disruptive innovation](#disruptive-innovation),
[Organizational ecology](#organizational-ecology) (Section \@ref(organizational-ecology)),
[Competitive dynamics](#competitive-dynamics) (Section \@ref(competitive-dynamics)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Joseph Schumpeter broke with the equilibrium economics of his day by arguing
that the essential feature of capitalism is not price competition among
identical firms but change from within. In *The Theory of Economic Development*
[@schumpeter1934] he defined development as the carrying out of **new
combinations**, and he listed five forms: a new good or a new quality of a good,
a new method of production, the opening of a new market, the conquest of a new
source of supply, and the reorganization of an industry, for example by creating
or breaking up a monopoly position. The agent who carries out new combinations
is the **entrepreneur**, a role defined by function rather than by ownership: a
manager who introduces a new combination is acting entrepreneurially, while a
capitalist who merely supplies funds is not.

Three decades later, *Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy* [@schumpeter1942]
gave the process its famous name. **Creative destruction** describes how new
goods, methods, and organizational forms incessantly revolutionize the economic
structure from within, destroying the old one and creating a new one. The book
also changed the protagonist. The lone entrepreneur of 1911 gave way to the
large corporation whose research laboratory routinizes innovation. Later
scholars labelled these two pictures *Schumpeter Mark I* (entry by new firms
drives innovation) and *Schumpeter Mark II* (established firms with large
research budgets drive it). Whether small or large firms innovate more remains
an active empirical question.

### Core logic and propositions

The logic can be stated as a short chain. Innovation creates a temporary
monopoly. The monopoly yields **innovation rents** (profits above the
competitive level). The rents attract imitators and further innovators, who
erode them and, in time, render the original innovation obsolete. Growth
therefore comes in waves of innovation, imitation, and replacement rather than
as a smooth accumulation of capital.

@aghion1992 built this idea into a formal model of economic growth. Research
firms compete to produce the next improvement in an intermediate good. Each
successful innovation makes the previous generation obsolete, so the innovator
earns monopoly profits only until the next innovation arrives. Two implications
follow. First, the expected value of research falls when future research is
expected to be intense, because rents will be short-lived. Second, private and
social returns to research diverge: innovators ignore the profits they destroy
for incumbents (the **business-stealing effect**) and the benefits their ideas
provide to future innovators (an intertemporal spillover). Equilibrium growth can
therefore be either too fast or too slow relative to the social optimum.

- **P1 (Rents drive effort).** Innovative effort increases with the size and
  expected duration of the rents an innovation can earn.
- **P2 (Obsolescence).** Each successful innovation reduces the value of the
  assets, skills, and firms tied to the technology it replaces.
- **P3 (Turnover).** Industries with higher rates of innovation exhibit higher
  rates of entry, exit, and turnover in market leadership.
- **P4 (Competition and innovation).** The effect of product-market competition
  on innovation is non-monotonic: competition encourages firms to innovate to
  escape rivals but reduces the rents that reward innovation.

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-ie-cd-cycle) summarizes the cycle. The dashed feedback edge
is the key to the dynamic: rents attract the next wave of innovators whose
success destroys the current incumbents.

```{r fig-ie-cd-cycle, fig.cap = "The cycle of creative destruction. A new combination yields temporary rents that attract imitators and new innovators. Their success erodes rents and makes the incumbent technology obsolete, restarting the cycle."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  E [label = "Entrepreneur or\\nR&D-intensive firm", %s]
  N [label = "New combination\\n(good, method, market,\\nsupply, organization)", %s]
  R [label = "Temporary\\ninnovation rents", %s]
  I [label = "Imitation and\\nnew entry", %s]
  O [label = "Obsolescence of\\nincumbent products\\nand firms", %s]
  C [label = "Appropriability and\\ncompetition intensity", %s]
  E -> N [label = " introduces"]
  N -> R
  R -> I [label = " attract"]
  I -> O [label = " erode and\\n displace"]
  O -> E [label = " next wave", style = dashed, constraint = false]
  C -> R [style = dotted, arrowhead = none]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

### Evidence and extensions

The macroeconomic literature on Schumpeterian growth has grown into a large
research programme that links innovation to firm entry, exit, and reallocation.
An influential empirical extension concerns P4. Using panel data on British
industries, @aghion2005 found an **inverted-U** relationship between
product-market competition and patenting. When competition is weak, more of it
spurs innovation because firms that innovate can escape their rivals. When
competition is already intense, more of it discourages innovation because
laggards expect little reward from catching up. The result reconciles the Mark I
view (competition spurs innovation) with the Mark II view (market power funds
it), at least in the setting studied.

At the firm level, creative destruction underpins much of the strategy
literature on technological change. @tushman1986 showed that discontinuous
technologies alter the competitive landscape of entire industries, and the
theories of [disruptive](#disruptive-innovation),
[architectural](#architectural-innovation), and
[competence-destroying](#dominant-design) change can be read as specifications
of *when* the destructive half of the process falls on incumbents.

::: {.debate}
**Is destruction the right word?** Critics note that many innovations
complement rather than replace existing assets, and that incumbents often
survive technological transitions by controlling complementary assets
[@tripsas1997; @teece1986]. In Tripsas's study of typesetting, incumbents
survived three generations of competence-destroying technology when they owned
specialized assets such as font libraries and sales networks. Creative
destruction is therefore best treated as a tendency whose incidence on
particular firms depends on the conditions specified by the more specific
theories below. A second debate is normative: because the Aghion and Howitt
model shows that equilibrium innovation can be either excessive or deficient,
the theory does not by itself justify either stronger or weaker patent
protection.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**The smartphone as a destroyer of categories.** The diffusion of smartphones
after 2007 illustrates every element of Schumpeter's account. A single new good
combined functions previously sold as separate products: standalone
satellite-navigation devices, compact digital cameras, portable music players,
and handheld game consoles. Each of these categories contracted as the
smartphone absorbed its function, and firms built around them had to reinvent
themselves or shrink. The same innovation created new industries (mobile apps,
ride-hailing, mobile payments) and new rents for the firms that controlled the
platform. For a strategist, the lesson is that the relevant competitive threat
may come not from a rival in one's own category but from a new combination that
makes the category unnecessary.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Industries with higher patenting intensity will exhibit higher annual
  turnover among the top four firms by market share.
- *H2.* The relationship between industry concentration and new-product
  introductions will be inverted-U shaped.

**Designs.** Firm and industry panels linking patents or product introductions
to entry, exit, and market-share turnover. Natural experiments that change
competitive pressure (trade liberalization, deregulation, patent-term changes).

**Measures.** Patent counts and forward citations, product-introduction
databases, firm entry and exit from business registers, rank turnover among
leaders, price-cost margins as a proxy for competition.
:::

## Disruptive Innovation {#disruptive-innovation}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Incumbents tend to win battles of **sustaining** innovation
that improve products along dimensions their best customers value, but they
tend to lose to **disruptive** innovations that start as inferior,
cheaper, or more convenient offerings for overlooked customers and then improve
until they satisfy the mainstream.

**Origins.** Strategy and technology management. @bower1995 introduced the
idea in practitioner form. @christensen1997 developed it from a study of the
disk-drive industry. @christensen2015 restated the theory and its boundaries.

**Level of analysis.** Firm and industry, with resource-allocation processes
inside the incumbent firm as the micro-mechanism.

**Key constructs.** Sustaining versus disruptive innovation, performance
trajectories, performance oversupply, value network, low-end and new-market
footholds, resource allocation.

**Boundary conditions.** Applies when technology improves faster than
mainstream customers' needs, when the entrant begins in a segment incumbents
find unattractive, and when incumbents' resource-allocation processes are tied
to existing customers and margins. Does not describe every successful entrant.

**Related theories.** [Exploration and exploitation](#exploration-exploitation) (Section \@ref(exploration-exploitation)),
[Ambidexterity](#ambidexterity) (Section \@ref(ambidexterity)), [Resource dependence theory](#resource-dependence-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-dependence-theory)),
[Architectural innovation](#architectural-innovation).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Clayton Christensen began with a puzzle from the disk-drive industry. Leading
manufacturers of 14-inch drives were technically excellent and closely attuned
to their customers, yet they missed the shift to 8-inch drives, whose early
products had lower capacity but suited the emerging minicomputer market. The
same pattern repeated at the transitions to 5.25-inch drives (desktop
computers) and 3.5-inch drives (portable computers). @christensen1995
introduced the concept of the **value network**, the context of customers,
suppliers, and cost structures within which a firm defines and solves problems,
and argued that incumbents fail when a technology's initial value lies outside
their value network. @christensen1996 traced the mechanism to **customer
power**: firms allocate resources to projects that their most profitable
customers demand, which starves projects aimed at small, low-margin markets.
@christensen1997 synthesized the argument in *The Innovator's Dilemma*.

### Core logic and propositions

The theory rests on two trajectories. The first is the trajectory of
**performance demanded** by customers in a market tier, which rises slowly. The
second is the trajectory of **performance supplied** by a technology, which
rises faster as firms pursue sustaining improvements. Because supply outpaces
demand, incumbents eventually **overshoot** what mainstream customers can use.
A disruptive entrant begins below mainstream needs but serves a foothold
market, either the least demanding customers (a **low-end foothold**) or people
who previously did not consume the product at all (a **new-market foothold**).
As the entrant's technology improves, it becomes good enough for the mainstream
while retaining its advantages in cost, simplicity, or convenience
[@christensen2015].

- **P1 (Sustaining advantage).** Incumbents usually prevail in sustaining
  innovations, whether incremental or radical, that serve their existing
  customers.
- **P2 (Overshooting).** When performance supplied exceeds performance
  demanded, the basis of competition shifts toward convenience, customization,
  and price.
- **P3 (Asymmetric motivation).** Incumbents rationally decline to pursue
  foothold markets because those markets are small and offer lower margins than
  the core business.
- **P4 (Process, not event).** Disruption unfolds over years. Its outcome
  depends on whether the entrant's trajectory reaches mainstream needs before
  incumbents respond.

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-ie-trajectories) reproduces the classic diagram with
stylised values.

```{r fig-ie-trajectories, fig.cap = "Stylised performance trajectories in disruptive innovation. Incumbents' sustaining improvements overshoot what mainstream customers can use, while a disruptive technology starts below mainstream needs and improves until it is good enough. Illustrative values only.", fig.height = 4.4}
set.seed(1997)
yrs <- seq(0, 20, by = 0.25)
traj <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(t = yrs, perf = 40 + 1.0 * yrs, series = "Mainstream customer needs"),
  data.frame(t = yrs, perf = 22 + 0.8 * yrs, series = "Low-end customer needs"),
  data.frame(t = yrs, perf = 45 + 3.2 * yrs, series = "Incumbent technology"),
  data.frame(t = yrs, perf = 8 + 3.4 * yrs, series = "Disruptive technology")
)
cross <- (40 - 8) / (3.4 - 1.0)
ggplot(traj, aes(t, perf, colour = series, linetype = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("point", x = cross, y = 40 + cross, size = 3, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = cross + 0.4, y = 40 + cross - 13, hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]],
           label = "Disruptive technology becomes\ngood enough for the mainstream") +
  annotate("text", x = 12.5, y = 104, hjust = 1, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]],
           label = "Performance oversupply") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Incumbent technology" = pal[["blue"]], "Disruptive technology" = pal[["orange"]],
                                 "Mainstream customer needs" = ink[["secondary"]], "Low-end customer needs" = ink[["muted"]])) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Incumbent technology" = "solid", "Disruptive technology" = "solid",
                                   "Mainstream customer needs" = "dashed", "Low-end customer needs" = "dotted")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 115)) +
  labs(x = "Time (years)", y = "Product performance (index)", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL,
       title = "Sustaining trajectories overshoot, disruptive ones catch up",
       caption = "Stylised: linear trajectories chosen for exposition, after Christensen (1997). Not empirical data.") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2), linetype = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

Table \@ref(tab:tab-ie-disruption-types) distinguishes the two footholds from
sustaining innovation.

```{r tab-ie-disruption-types}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Dimension, ~`Sustaining innovation`, ~`Low-end disruption`, ~`New-market disruption`,
  "Target customers", "Most demanding, most profitable customers", "Over-served customers at the bottom of the market", "Non-consumers who lacked money, skill, or access",
  "Initial performance", "Better on established attributes", "Good enough on established attributes", "Worse on established attributes, better on new ones",
  "Business model", "Existing margins and cost structure", "Lower cost, lower price", "New value network",
  "Incumbent response", "Fight and usually win", "Retreat up-market to protect margins", "Ignore, because the market looks small",
  "Examples discussed in the literature", "Successive gains in drive capacity", "Minimills in steel", "Personal computers relative to minicomputers"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Sustaining innovation and the two forms of disruption (after Christensen, Raynor, & McDonald, 2015).")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The disk-drive evidence in @christensen1997 remains the core of the theory, and
@christensen1995 and @christensen1996 provide the more formal academic
statements. @henderson1993 offered a complementary analysis of
photolithographic equipment, arguing that incumbents' failures reflected both
rational **underinvestment**, because new technologies cannibalize existing
rents, and organizational **incompetence**, because embedded routines hinder
new learning. That distinction matters: a theory of incentives implies that
incumbents *choose* not to respond, whereas a theory of capabilities implies
that they *cannot*. The managerial prescription in @christensen1997, an
autonomous unit with a cost structure suited to the new market, addresses both,
and it anticipates the literature on structural [ambidexterity](#ambidexterity) (Section \@ref(ambidexterity)).

::: {.debate}
**How useful is the theory of disruptive innovation?** In a widely read essay,
@lepore2014 criticized the theory's case selection, argued that several firms
described as disrupted had in fact prospered, and questioned whether the theory
could predict rather than merely redescribe. @king2015 asked experts to assess
cases cited as disruptions in Christensen's books against the theory's core
conditions, such as incumbents overshooting customer needs and having the
capability to respond but failing to do so, and found that only a small minority
of cases met all of them. @christensen2015 replied in part by narrowing the
concept: disruption refers to a process that starts from a low-end or
new-market foothold, and many successful entrants (they cite Uber in its home
market) are not disruptive in this sense. The exchange illustrates a general
lesson about theory from Chapter 2: a concept stretched to cover every case
loses its explanatory power. Scholars who use the theory should measure its
conditions rather than infer them from outcomes.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Netflix and Blockbuster.** @christensen2015 use Netflix as an example of
disruption done right. Its DVD-by-mail service, launched in the late 1990s,
appealed to a small set of customers, among them early adopters of DVD players
and online shoppers, but did not suit the typical Blockbuster customer who
wanted a new release on impulse. Blockbuster had little reason to respond.
Netflix's move to streaming then improved the offering until it served the
mainstream, and Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy in 2010. The case is analysed
from the perspective of capability renewal in Chapter 5 (see
[Dynamic capabilities](#dynamic-capabilities-framework) (Section \@ref(dynamic-capabilities-framework))). Read through
disruption theory, the instructive feature is that Netflix's initial *inferiority*
on immediacy was what kept the incumbent from fighting back.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Incumbents will be slower to enter a new product segment when the
  segment's initial customers overlap little with their existing customer base.
- *H2.* The hazard of incumbent exit after the entry of a low-cost technology
  will be higher when the incumbent's products exceed the performance demanded
  by the median customer.

**Designs.** Industry histories that code product performance and customer
requirements over time. Event-history models of incumbent entry into new
segments. Pre-registered *ex ante* classification of innovations as sustaining
or disruptive, followed by prospective tracking.

**Measures.** Product performance on key attributes, customer-requirement
surveys, overlap between new-segment and core customers, internal resource
allocation to new versus core projects.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Calling every successful entrant disruptive.** Disruption is a specific
process with stated conditions: an inferior foothold product, a faster-improving
trajectory, and an incumbent with rational reasons not to respond. Labelling a
case "disruptive" because the incumbent lost is circular. Classify innovations
before outcomes are known and report the cases that did not follow the
predicted path.
:::

## Profiting from Innovation {#profiting-from-innovation}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Innovators often fail to profit from their innovations. Whether
the innovator, imitators, or the owners of complementary assets capture the
value depends on the **appropriability regime**, the stage of the **dominant
design**, and access to **complementary assets**.

**Origins.** Strategy and industrial organization. @teece1986, revisited in
@teece2006.

**Level of analysis.** Firm (innovator, imitator, asset owner) within an
industry.

**Key constructs.** Appropriability regime (tight or weak), legal protection,
tacit versus codified knowledge, pre-paradigmatic and paradigmatic phases,
complementary assets (generic, specialized, cospecialized), contracting versus
integration.

**Boundary conditions.** Most relevant for product and process innovations
that require downstream manufacturing, distribution, or service to reach
customers. Less relevant for innovations sold as pure intellectual property in
efficient markets for technology.

**Related theories.** [Resource-based theory](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)),
[Transaction cost economics](#transaction-cost-economics) (Section \@ref(transaction-cost-economics)),
[First-mover advantage](#first-mover-advantage) (Section \@ref(first-mover-advantage)),
[Network effects](#network-effects) (Section \@ref(network-effects)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

@teece1986 began from a set of puzzling outcomes. EMI invented the CT scanner
and lost the market. RC Cola introduced diet cola before Coca-Cola and Pepsi,
yet the large brands dominated the category. Other pioneers, such as Pilkington
with float glass, did capture the value of their inventions. Teece argued that
these outcomes are not accidents of management but reflect three structural
features of the innovation's environment. The article became one of the most
cited in strategic management and laid foundations for later work on
ecosystems, platforms, and [dynamic capabilities](#dynamic-capabilities-framework) (Section \@ref(dynamic-capabilities-framework))
[@teece2006].

### Core logic and propositions

The first building block is the **appropriability regime**: the extent to which
the innovator can prevent imitation. It depends on legal instruments (patents,
copyright, trade secrets) and on the nature of the knowledge. Tacit knowledge
that is hard to articulate is easier to protect than codified knowledge that can
be read from a product or a patent. Regimes are **tight** when imitation is
difficult and **weak** when it is easy. Teece stressed that tight regimes are
the exception: in most industries patents are easy to invent around.

The second is the **dominant design paradigm**. Early in an industry's life
(the pre-paradigmatic phase), many designs compete. Once a dominant design
emerges, competition shifts to price and scale. An innovator with a weak regime
may find that its early design is not the one that wins (see
[Dominant design](#dominant-design)).

The third is **complementary assets**: the capabilities and assets needed to
commercialize an innovation, such as manufacturing, distribution, service,
brand, and complementary technologies. **Generic** assets are available on
competitive terms. **Specialized** assets have a one-way dependence with the
innovation. **Cospecialized** assets have a mutual dependence. When the regime
is weak and the needed complementary assets are specialized and scarce, the
owners of those assets are in a strong bargaining position and capture much
of the value.

- **P1 (Tight regimes favour innovators).** Under a tight appropriability
  regime, the innovator is likely to capture a large share of the value it
  creates, whether by producing or by licensing.
- **P2 (Weak regimes and timing).** Under a weak regime, the innovator's
  position deteriorates once a dominant design emerges and competition shifts
  to complementary assets.
- **P3 (Asset ownership).** When complementary assets are specialized and
  scarce, owners of those assets (incumbents or fast followers) tend to capture
  value at the innovator's expense.
- **P4 (Integration choice).** An innovator should integrate into specialized
  complementary assets when the regime is weak, the assets are critical, and
  the innovator can afford to build or buy them in time, and should contract for
  them otherwise.

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-ie-pfi-logic) expresses the argument as a decision logic.

```{r fig-ie-pfi-logic, fig.cap = "The logic of profiting from innovation. Tight appropriability favours the innovator. Under weak appropriability, value flows to whoever controls specialized complementary assets once a dominant design has emerged. Adapted from the argument in Teece (1986).", fig.height = 5}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  A [label = "Innovation\\ncommercialized", %s]
  Q1 [label = "Appropriability\\nregime tight?", %s]
  W1 [label = "Innovator well placed\\n(produce or license)", %s]
  Q2 [label = "Specialized complementary\\nassets needed and scarce?", %s]
  W2 [label = "Contract for generic assets.\\nRents compete away to\\nimitators and customers", %s]
  Q3 [label = "Innovator owns or can\\nbuild them before the\\ndominant design emerges?", %s]
  W3 [label = "Innovator captures value\\n(integrate)", %s]
  W4 [label = "Owners of complementary\\nassets capture value", %s]
  A -> Q1
  Q1 -> W1 [label = " yes"]
  Q1 -> Q2 [label = " no"]
  Q2 -> W2 [label = " no"]
  Q2 -> Q3 [label = " yes"]
  Q3 -> W3 [label = " yes"]
  Q3 -> W4 [label = " no"]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_outcome),
rankdir = "TB", height = 520)
```

Table \@ref(tab:tab-ie-pfi-winners) summarizes who tends to win under each
configuration, with examples Teece discussed.

```{r tab-ie-pfi-winners}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Configuration, ~`Likely winner`, ~Reason, ~`Example in Teece (1986)`,
  "Tight regime, any asset position", "Innovator", "Imitation is blocked, so the innovator can produce or license on favourable terms", "Pilkington float glass",
  "Weak regime, generic complementary assets", "Customers and many imitators", "Anyone can copy and contract for the assets, so rents compete away", "Many consumer products after a design stabilizes",
  "Weak regime, specialized assets held by innovator", "Innovator", "Imitators cannot reach customers without assets the innovator controls", "Integrated firms that own manufacturing and distribution",
  "Weak regime, specialized assets held by others", "Imitators or asset owners", "Owners of manufacturing, brand, distribution, or service extract the value", "EMI and the CT scanner, RC Cola and diet cola",
  "Pre-paradigmatic phase, weak regime", "Uncertain", "The innovator's design may not become dominant, and positioning for the eventual design matters most", "Early entrants in many new product categories"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Who profits from innovation? Configurations in Teece's framework.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

@tripsas1997 provided some of the most careful evidence. Across a century of
the typesetter industry, incumbents that held specialized complementary assets
survived waves of competence-destroying technology that would otherwise have
removed them. @gans2003 extended the framework to entrepreneurial strategy: a
start-up should cooperate with incumbents (for instance by licensing or being
acquired) when its intellectual property is strong and incumbents control the
needed complementary assets, and compete in the product market when neither
holds. In his reflections, @teece2006 noted that the framework anticipated later
work on business ecosystems and platforms, where control of a few critical
complements, such as an operating system or an app store, can determine who
captures value from many other firms' innovations.

::: {.debate}
**How weak are weak regimes?** Teece's emphasis on complementary assets assumes
that patents are usually weak. In pharmaceuticals and specialty chemicals,
patents are strong and innovators often capture value through licensing. In
software and digital services, by contrast, network effects and data can act
as complementary assets that are themselves created by the innovation, blurring
the line between the innovation and its complements. Critics also note that the
framework is easier to apply in hindsight than in prospect, because which
assets will become specialized depends on which design wins.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**EMI and the CT scanner.** EMI's scanner was a genuine breakthrough, but
selling and supporting sophisticated equipment to hospitals required a sales
force, service network, and relationships with radiologists, especially in the
United States, that established medical-electronics firms possessed and EMI did
not. The underlying ideas could be engineered around. Firms with those
complementary assets, including General Electric, entered quickly, and EMI
exited the scanner business within a decade of launch [@teece1986]. The lesson
is not that EMI should not have innovated but that its commercialization
strategy needed either a partner that owned the complementary assets or an
early, deliberate investment in building them.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**The iPhone and complementary assets.** Apple's 2007 iPhone was neither the
first smartphone nor the first touchscreen phone, and many of its features were
quickly imitated. Yet Apple has captured a share of industry profits well above
its share of unit sales. Teece's framework explains why. Apple held a portfolio
of complementary assets that rivals could not easily replicate: a premium brand,
its own retail stores (opened from 2001), the iTunes content and payment
infrastructure, deep supply-chain relationships, and, from 2008, the App Store,
which turned third-party developers into cospecialized complements. As a dominant
design for touchscreen smartphones emerged, competition shifted to exactly these
assets. Apple was a follower in the product category but an innovator in
assembling complements around it.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The positive effect of being first to market on long-run market share
  will be weaker when patent protection in the industry is weak.
- *H2.* Technology start-ups will be more likely to license or be acquired than
  to enter the product market when incumbents control specialized
  manufacturing or distribution assets.

**Designs.** Industry histories with event-history models of survival,
comparisons across industries that differ in patent effectiveness, and
commercialization-mode choice models for start-ups.

**Measures.** Survey measures of appropriability (patent effectiveness, secrecy,
lead time), ownership of downstream assets (sales force, service network,
manufacturing plants), licensing and acquisition events.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Equating invention with value capture.** Many business plans assume that a
patent or a technical lead guarantees profits. Teece's framework implies that
the right question is "Who controls the assets needed to bring this to
customers, and what happens after the design stabilizes?" Map the complementary
assets before choosing whether to build, partner, or license.
:::

## Architectural Innovation {#architectural-innovation}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Innovations that reconfigure how existing components are linked
together, while leaving the components largely unchanged, can destroy the value
of incumbents' **architectural knowledge** and are especially hard for
incumbents to recognize and exploit.

**Origins.** Technology management. @henderson1990, based on the
photolithographic alignment equipment industry.

**Level of analysis.** Product and firm, with the organization's communication
channels and information filters as the micro-mechanism.

**Key constructs.** Component knowledge, architectural knowledge, core design
concepts, linkages, incremental, modular, architectural, and radical
innovation, communication channels, information filters, problem-solving
strategies.

**Boundary conditions.** Applies to complex products made of interacting
components, developed by organizations whose structure mirrors the product's
architecture.

**Related theories.** [Disruptive innovation](#disruptive-innovation),
[Absorptive capacity](#absorptive-capacity) (Section \@ref(absorptive-capacity)),
[Knowledge-based view](#knowledge-based-view) (Section \@ref(knowledge-based-view)),
[Dominant design](#dominant-design).
:::

### Core logic

Earlier research had classified innovations as **incremental** or **radical**.
@henderson1990 observed that this dichotomy could not explain why incumbents
sometimes failed in the face of seemingly modest innovations. They argued that
designing a product requires two kinds of knowledge: **component knowledge**
about each core concept and how it is implemented, and **architectural
knowledge** about how components are integrated into a coherent whole. Crossing
these dimensions yields four types of innovation, shown in Figure
\@ref(fig:fig-ie-hc-matrix).

```{r fig-ie-hc-matrix, fig.cap = "Henderson and Clark's (1990) typology of innovation. Architectural innovation leaves core concepts intact but changes how components are linked, which is why incumbents often misread it as incremental.", fig.height = 4.4}
hc <- data.frame(
  x = c(1, 2, 1, 2), y = c(1, 1, 2, 2),
  type = c("Incremental", "Modular", "Architectural", "Radical"),
  desc = c("Refines components within\nan established design",
           "Replaces a core concept\nwithin an unchanged architecture",
           "Reconfigures links between\nexisting components",
           "New core concepts linked\nin a new architecture")
)
ggplot(hc, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = type), colour = "white", linewidth = 2, width = 0.98, height = 0.98, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_text(aes(label = type), fontface = "bold", size = 4.6, nudge_y = 0.17, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  geom_text(aes(label = desc), size = 3.3, nudge_y = -0.12, colour = ink[["secondary"]], lineheight = 0.95) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Incremental" = "#eef4fb", "Modular" = "#e8f6ef",
                               "Architectural" = "#fff4e5", "Radical" = "#f4f0ff"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:2, labels = c("Reinforced", "Overturned"), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:2, labels = c("Unchanged", "Changed"), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Core design concepts", y = "Linkages between core\nconcepts and components",
       title = "Four types of innovation",
       caption = "Typology from Henderson and Clark (1990). Cell descriptions paraphrased.") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text = element_text(size = 11))
```

Their own example is the room fan. Improving blade design or motor power within
a standard ceiling fan is incremental. Replacing the motor with a fundamentally
different one is modular. Designing a portable fan, which uses largely the same
components but arranges them in a different configuration with different
interactions among blade size, motor power, and housing, is architectural.

The difficulty for incumbents is that architectural knowledge becomes embedded
in the organization. Teams are structured around components, **communication
channels** link the people whose components interact, **information filters**
highlight the variables that matter in the existing design, and
**problem-solving strategies** become routine. Because these structures were
built for the old architecture, they screen out precisely the information that
signals a new one. An incumbent may therefore treat an architectural innovation
as incremental, apply its familiar routines, and fail.

- **P1.** Incumbents are more likely to fail in architectural and radical
  innovations than in incremental and modular ones.
- **P2.** The more an organization's communication structure mirrors the
  existing product architecture, the harder it is to recognize architectural
  change.
- **P3.** Architectural innovation is more damaging than its technical
  magnitude suggests because it is often misclassified as incremental (Table \@ref(tab:tab-ie-hc-types)).

```{r tab-ie-hc-types}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Type, ~`Component knowledge`, ~`Architectural knowledge`, ~`Typical incumbent outcome`, ~`Illustrative example`,
  "Incremental", "Enhanced", "Enhanced", "Incumbent advantage", "Successive improvements in a standard product",
  "Modular", "Destroyed", "Enhanced", "Incumbents can adapt by acquiring new component skills", "Replacing an analogue component with a digital one",
  "Architectural", "Largely enhanced", "Destroyed", "Often fail, because the change is misread", "Room fan to portable fan, contact to proximity aligners",
  "Radical", "Destroyed", "Destroyed", "Usually fail, but the threat is recognized", "Shift to an entirely new technology base"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Knowledge effects of the four innovation types (after Henderson & Clark, 1990).")
```

### Evidence and extensions

In the photolithographic alignment equipment industry, a series of innovations
that appeared modest in technical terms (for example, the move from contact to
proximity aligners) was accompanied by changes in industry leadership, with
established firms repeatedly losing to entrants [@henderson1990;
@henderson1993]. The concept has since been used to explain organizational
design: firms that separate component development into modules may innovate
quickly within the architecture but struggle to change it. It links naturally to
[absorptive capacity](#absorptive-capacity) (Section \@ref(absorptive-capacity)) [@cohen1990], because recognizing
architectural change requires knowledge outside the current filters.

::: {.debate}
**Architecture or cognition?** Henderson and Clark locate the problem in
organizational structure and routines. Later work emphasized managerial
cognition. In their study of Polaroid's move into digital imaging,
@tripsas2000 found that the firm built strong technical capabilities but that
managers' beliefs about the business model held it back. The two explanations
are complementary but imply different remedies: restructuring communication
channels versus changing managers' mental models.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Kodak and the architecture of photography.** Digital imaging was radical for
Kodak's chemistry, but it was also architectural for the photography business.
The value chain shifted from film, processing, and prints to sensors, software,
storage, and screens, and later to sharing through smartphones and social media.
Kodak built an early digital camera in 1975 and invested in digital products,
yet its organization, profit model, and information filters remained centred on
film and photofinishing. @lucas2009 attribute the failure less to ignorance of
the technology than to an organization and culture unable to reconfigure around
it. The company filed for Chapter 11 protection in 2012. The capability side of
the story is covered in Chapter 5 under
[Dynamic capabilities](#dynamic-capabilities-framework) (Section \@ref(dynamic-capabilities-framework)). The architectural lens
adds that the hardest part to change was not knowledge of components but
knowledge of how the business fitted together.
:::

## Dominant Design and Technology Cycles {#dominant-design}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** New industries begin with a period of experimentation in which
many designs compete. A **dominant design** eventually emerges, after which the
focus of innovation shifts from product to process, the number of firms falls,
and competition turns to cost and scale until a new technological
discontinuity restarts the cycle.

**Origins.** Technology management. @utterback1975 and @abernathy1978 on the
dynamics of product and process innovation. @tushman1986 and @anderson1990 on
technological discontinuities and technology cycles. Synthesized in
@utterback1994.

**Level of analysis.** Industry and technology, with consequences for firm
entry, exit, and survival.

**Key constructs.** Fluid, transitional, and specific phases, product versus
process innovation, dominant design, era of ferment, era of incremental change,
competence-enhancing versus competence-destroying discontinuities.

**Boundary conditions.** Fits assembled products with many interacting
components better than non-assembled goods or services. The concept of a single
dominant design is harder to apply in software and platform markets with
continual updates.

**Related theories.** [Product life cycle](#product-life-cycle) (Section \@ref(product-life-cycle)),
[Network effects](#network-effects) (Section \@ref(network-effects)), [Organizational ecology](#organizational-ecology) (Section \@ref(organizational-ecology)),
[Profiting from innovation](#profiting-from-innovation).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

@utterback1975 proposed that the rate and type of innovation in a productive
unit change as the unit matures. Early on, when performance requirements are
unclear, firms experiment with product features, and production processes are
flexible and inefficient. As the market learns what it wants, a design
stabilizes, and innovation shifts to the production process, which becomes more
specialized, capital-intensive, and efficient. @abernathy1978 named the three
stages the **fluid**, **transitional**, and **specific** phases and illustrated
them with the automobile industry, in which Ford's Model T became a dominant
design around which mass production was organized.

### Core logic and propositions

A **dominant design** is the configuration that wins allegiance in the
marketplace and that competitors and innovators must adhere to if they hope to
command significant market share. It is rarely the most advanced technology.
It usually combines features pioneered by several firms, and it can be shaped by
network effects, complementary assets, regulation, and alliances as much as by
technical merit [@anderson1990]. Examples often given include the QWERTY
typewriter keyboard, the Model T, the VHS video format, and the IBM-compatible
personal computer.

@anderson1990 embedded the concept in a **technology cycle**. A technological
discontinuity opens an **era of ferment** marked by competition among variants
of the new technology and between the new and old technologies. The selection of
a dominant design ends the era of ferment and opens an **era of incremental
change**, which lasts until the next discontinuity. @tushman1986 added that
discontinuities differ in their effect on incumbents. **Competence-enhancing**
discontinuities build on existing know-how and tend to be introduced by
incumbents. **Competence-destroying** discontinuities render existing know-how
obsolete and tend to be introduced by new entrants.

- **P1 (Phase shift).** The rate of product innovation peaks before the
  emergence of a dominant design, and the rate of process innovation peaks after
  it.
- **P2 (Shakeout).** The number of firms in an industry rises during the era of
  ferment and falls sharply after a dominant design emerges.
- **P3 (Competence effects).** Competence-destroying discontinuities increase
  the share of new entrants among industry leaders, and competence-enhancing
  discontinuities consolidate incumbents' positions.
- **P4 (Selection is social).** Which design becomes dominant cannot be
  predicted from technical merit alone.

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-ie-au-model) shows the stylised pattern behind P1.

```{r fig-ie-au-model, fig.cap = "Stylised Abernathy-Utterback dynamics. Product innovation dominates the fluid phase. After a dominant design emerges, the rate of process innovation peaks and both rates eventually decline. Illustrative curves only.", fig.height = 4.2}
tt <- seq(0, 30, by = 0.2)
au <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(t = tt, rate = 100 * dgamma(tt, shape = 2.2, scale = 3.2) / max(dgamma(tt, shape = 2.2, scale = 3.2)),
             series = "Product innovation"),
  data.frame(t = tt, rate = 85 * dgamma(tt, shape = 5, scale = 3.4) / max(dgamma(tt, shape = 5, scale = 3.4)),
             series = "Process innovation")
)
ggplot(au, aes(t, rate, colour = series)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 9, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = pal[["blue"]], alpha = 0.06) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 9, xmax = 19, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = pal[["yellow"]], alpha = 0.06) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 19, xmax = 30, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = pal[["aqua"]], alpha = 0.06) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 9, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = c(4.5, 14, 24.5), y = 112, label = c("Fluid phase", "Transitional phase", "Specific phase"),
           size = 3.4, colour = ink[["secondary"]], fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 9.3, y = 96, label = "Dominant design\nemerges", hjust = 0, size = 3.1, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Product innovation" = pal[["blue"]], "Process innovation" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 118), breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)) +
  labs(x = "Time since the industry's origin (years)", y = "Rate of major innovation (index)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Product innovation gives way to process innovation",
       caption = "Stylised curves after Utterback and Abernathy (1975) and Abernathy and Utterback (1978). Not empirical data.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The empirical record broadly supports the cycle. @anderson1990 found the
predicted sequence of discontinuity, ferment, and dominant design in the cement,
glass, and minicomputer industries, and reported that the dominant design was
seldom the technological frontier at the time of the discontinuity.
@suarez1995 showed that the emergence of a dominant design shapes firm
survival: across several industries, firms that entered before a dominant
design emerged had better survival prospects than those that entered after.
@klepper1996 offered an economic explanation for shakeouts in which larger firms
gain more from process innovation because they spread its cost over more output,
so that early entrants that grow large come to dominate.

::: {.debate}
**Is the dominant design a cause or a label?** Critics point out that a
dominant design is often identified only after the shakeout it is supposed to
explain, which risks circularity. Others argue that in modular, software-based
products, architectures evolve continuously and the cycle compresses or blurs.
The competence-destroying versus competence-enhancing distinction has also been
challenged: whether a technology destroys a firm's competence depends on the
particular firm, as the typesetter evidence on complementary assets shows
[@tripsas1997]. The most defensible use of the framework is as a set of
conditional expectations about where an industry is in its cycle, not as a
deterministic timetable.
:::

Table \@ref(tab:tab-ie-competence) presents the competence-enhancing versus competence-destroying discontinuities (after Tushman & Anderson, 1986).

```{r tab-ie-competence}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Feature, ~`Competence-enhancing discontinuity`, ~`Competence-destroying discontinuity`,
  "Effect on know-how", "Builds on existing skills and knowledge", "Makes existing skills and knowledge obsolete",
  "Typical initiator", "Incumbent firms", "New entrants",
  "Effect on industry structure", "Reinforces incumbents' positions", "Opens the door to new leaders",
  "Managerial challenge", "Keep investing in the current trajectory", "Recognize the threat and build or buy new competences",
  "Link to other theories", "[Profiting from innovation](#profiting-from-innovation): incumbents' assets retain value", "[Creative destruction](#creative-destruction), [Liability of newness](#liability-of-newness) for entrants"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Competence-enhancing versus competence-destroying discontinuities (after Tushman & Anderson, 1986).")
```

::: {.business-case}
**Format battles and the timing of commitment.** In consumer electronics, the
contest between VHS and Betamax in home video is a frequently cited case in
which the eventual dominant design was not universally judged the technically
superior one. Its victory owed much to licensing, recording time, and the
availability of pre-recorded content: network effects and complementary assets
rather than picture quality. For managers, the cycle has two practical
implications. During the era of ferment, invest in flexibility and alliances
that improve the odds of being on the winning design. Once a design is dominant,
shift resources to process efficiency, cost, and the complementary assets that
will determine profits.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* After a dominant design emerges, the ratio of process to product patents
  in an industry will increase.
- *H2.* Firms entering an industry after the emergence of a dominant design will
  face a higher hazard of exit than firms that entered before it.

**Designs.** Long industry histories coded from trade directories, product
catalogues, and patent data. Event-history models of entry and exit. Content
analysis of product specifications to date dominant designs independently of
outcomes.

**Measures.** Product-feature convergence across models, process versus product
patent classes, number of producers over time, entry cohorts.
:::

## Open Innovation {#open-innovation}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Firms can and should use purposive inflows and outflows of
knowledge, bringing in external ideas and taking internal ideas to market
through external paths, rather than relying solely on internal research and
development.

**Origins.** Technology management. @chesbrough2003, building on earlier work
on absorptive capacity and user innovation. @laursen2006 on the returns to
external search. @dahlander2010 on the forms of openness.

**Level of analysis.** Firm, and its relations with universities, suppliers,
customers, start-ups, and communities.

**Key constructs.** Closed versus open innovation, inbound and outbound
openness, search breadth and depth, pecuniary and non-pecuniary exchange,
intellectual-property management, absorptive capacity.

**Boundary conditions.** Valuable where useful knowledge is widely distributed
and markets for technology function. Less valuable where knowledge is highly
tacit, integration costs are high, or appropriability concerns dominate.

**Related theories.** [Absorptive capacity](#absorptive-capacity) (Section \@ref(absorptive-capacity)),
[Structural holes](#structural-holes) (Section \@ref(structural-holes)), [Social capital](#social-capital) (Section \@ref(social-capital)),
[Profiting from innovation](#profiting-from-innovation).
:::

### Core logic

@chesbrough2003 contrasted two paradigms. Under **closed innovation**, a firm
generates its own ideas, develops them in its own laboratories, and brings them
to market through its own channels. Under **open innovation**, the boundary of
the firm is porous: valuable ideas can come from outside, and internal ideas
that do not fit the current business can reach the market through licensing,
spin-offs, or partnerships. Chesbrough argued that several erosion factors had
undermined the closed model, notably the growing mobility of skilled workers,
the availability of venture capital for spin-offs, and the rising capability of
external suppliers and universities. His cautionary example was Xerox's Palo
Alto Research Center, which generated influential technologies whose value was
largely captured by other firms (Table \@ref(tab:tab-ie-open-closed)).

```{r tab-ie-open-closed}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Principle, ~`Closed innovation`, ~`Open innovation`,
  "Source of talent", "The best people in the field work for us", "Not all the best people work for us, so we must work with those outside",
  "Profiting from R&D", "We must discover, develop, and ship it ourselves", "External R&D can create value, and internal R&D captures part of it",
  "Speed to market", "Being first to discover wins", "Building a better business model beats being first to discover",
  "Intellectual property", "Control it so competitors cannot benefit", "Profit from others' use of our IP and buy others' IP when it advances our model",
  "Unused ideas", "Shelved", "Licensed, spun off, or contributed to partners"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Closed versus open innovation (principles paraphrased from Chesbrough, 2003).")
```

@dahlander2010 clarified that openness comes in four forms by crossing
direction with exchange type. **Inbound** openness includes *sourcing* external
knowledge without payment (for example from users or scientific publications)
and *acquiring* it through licences or purchases. **Outbound** openness includes
*revealing* internal knowledge without immediate payment and *selling* it
through licences or spin-offs. Each form has distinct costs and benefits.

### Evidence and extensions

@laursen2006 studied how the **breadth** (number of external sources used) and
**depth** (intensity of use) of external search relate to innovation
performance among UK manufacturing firms. Both were positively associated with
the share of sales from new products, but with diminishing and eventually
negative returns: an **inverted-U**. The explanation is attention. Each
additional external relationship demands managerial time to identify, absorb,
and integrate knowledge, and beyond some point the costs exceed the benefits.
Figure \@ref(fig:fig-ie-open-u) shows the shape with simulated data.

```{r fig-ie-open-u, fig.cap = "Illustrative simulation of the inverted-U relationship between breadth of external search and innovation performance reported by Laursen and Salter (2006). Points are simulated firms, the line is a quadratic fit.", fig.height = 4}
set.seed(2006)
n_firms <- 400
breadth <- sample(0:16, n_firms, replace = TRUE)
perf <- 8 + 3.2 * breadth - 0.16 * breadth^2 + rnorm(n_firms, 0, 4)
open_df <- data.frame(breadth, perf = pmax(perf, 0))
peak <- 3.2 / (2 * 0.16)
ggplot(open_df, aes(breadth, perf)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.18, height = 0, alpha = 0.35, colour = pal[["blue"]], size = 1.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ poly(x, 2), se = TRUE, colour = pal[["orange"]], fill = pal[["orange"]], alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = peak, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = peak + 0.3, y = 3, hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]],
           label = "Returns turn negative:\nover-search") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 16, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Breadth of external search (number of source types used)",
       y = "Innovation performance\n(share of sales from new products, %)",
       title = "Openness helps, up to a point",
       caption = "Stylised simulation (n = 400 firms). Shape follows Laursen and Salter (2006). Values are not estimates.")
```

Open innovation intersects with [absorptive capacity](#absorptive-capacity) (Section \@ref(absorptive-capacity)):
firms need internal research to recognize and assimilate outside knowledge
[@cohen1990]. It also connects to network theories, since external search
draws on brokers and bridging ties (see [Structural holes](#structural-holes) (Section \@ref(structural-holes))).

::: {.debate}
**Is open innovation new?** Critics argue that firms have long sourced ideas
externally through acquisitions, licensing, and collaboration, and that open
innovation relabels familiar practices. Defenders respond that the contribution
lies in treating openness as a deliberate strategy with its own business model,
and in measuring its forms and limits. A second concern is appropriability:
revealing knowledge can help rivals as much as partners, which ties the theory
back to [Profiting from innovation](#profiting-from-innovation).
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Procter & Gamble's Connect and Develop.** In the early 2000s, P&G's leadership
concluded that internal research alone could not deliver the growth the company
needed. It set a goal of sourcing half of its innovations from outside the
company and created a programme, Connect and Develop, that used technology
scouts, supplier networks, and online intermediaries to find external solutions
to defined problems. @huston2006, two P&G executives, describe how the firm
specified needs in short technology briefs and searched its networks for
existing solutions. One example they report is Pringles crisps printed with
pictures and words, which used an ink-jet technique developed by a small bakery
in Italy rather than one invented in-house. The programme illustrates inbound,
pecuniary openness and the importance of internal capability to evaluate what
is found outside.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The relationship between the number of external knowledge sources and
  new-product sales will be inverted-U shaped.
- *H2.* The optimal breadth of search will be higher for firms with greater
  internal R&D intensity (absorptive capacity).

**Designs.** Innovation surveys (such as the European Community Innovation
Survey) with breadth and depth indices, panel studies of licensing and
alliance portfolios, field studies of crowdsourcing contests.

**Measures.** Count of external source types used, intensity of use, in- and
out-licensing revenues, share of new products with external origins.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**More openness is always better.** Openness has costs in attention,
coordination, and appropriability. Firms that multiply partnerships without the
capacity to absorb them can see innovation performance fall. Treat openness as
a portfolio with an optimum, not a slogan.
:::

## Effectuation {#effectuation}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Under uncertainty, expert entrepreneurs often reason
**effectually**: they start from the means they control and let goals emerge
through commitments with stakeholders, rather than reasoning **causally** from a
predetermined goal to the means needed to reach it.

**Origins.** Entrepreneurship and cognitive science. @sarasvathy2001, drawing on
think-aloud protocols with expert entrepreneurs and on Herbert Simon's work on
decision making. Elaborated in @sarasvathy2008.

**Level of analysis.** Individual entrepreneur and the venture's stakeholder
network.

**Key constructs.** Causation, effectuation, means (who I am, what I know, whom
I know), affordable loss, partnerships and pre-commitments, leveraging
contingencies, non-predictive control.

**Boundary conditions.** Most applicable when the future is unpredictable, goals
are ambiguous, and the environment is shaped by the actions of the participants
(Knightian uncertainty). Causal reasoning is more effective when the market
exists and outcomes are predictable.

**Related theories.** [Bounded rationality](#bounded-rationality) (Section \@ref(bounded-rationality)),
[Real options theory](#real-options-theory) (Section \@ref(real-options-theory)),
[Opportunity discovery and creation](#opportunity-discovery-creation),
[Bricolage](#bricolage).
:::

### Origins and core logic

@sarasvathy2001 illustrated the difference with a chef. A chef reasoning
causally is given a menu and buys the ingredients needed to cook it. A chef
reasoning effectually looks in the cupboards and asks what meals can be made
with what is there. Both are rational, but they suit different conditions.
Causation is a logic of **prediction**: to the extent we can predict the
future, we can control it. Effectuation is a logic of **control**: to the extent
we can control the future, we do not need to predict it.

Sarasvathy's later work organized effectuation into a set of principles that
are now standard in entrepreneurship teaching [@sarasvathy2008] (Table \@ref(tab:tab-ie-effectuation)).

```{r tab-ie-effectuation}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Principle, ~`Effectual logic`, ~`Causal contrast`, ~`Business illustration`,
  "Bird in hand (means)", "Start with who you are, what you know, and whom you know", "Start with a goal and acquire the means to reach it", "A founder builds a product for the industry she has worked in for a decade",
  "Affordable loss", "Commit what you can afford to lose", "Pursue the option with the highest expected return", "Testing a concept with a weekend pop-up rather than a leased store",
  "Crazy quilt (partnerships)", "Bring in self-selected stakeholders who make commitments and shape goals", "Analyse competitors and position against them", "An early customer co-funds development in exchange for exclusivity",
  "Lemonade (contingencies)", "Treat surprises as resources to exploit", "Avoid deviations from the plan", "A failed feature reveals a different, more valuable use",
  "Pilot in the plane (control)", "Shape the future through action rather than forecast it", "Forecast the market and plan for it", "Creating an industry standard with partners instead of predicting one"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Principles of effectuation contrasted with causal reasoning (labels from Sarasvathy, 2008).")
```

### Mechanism

Effectuation describes a process rather than a single decision. Means suggest
possible courses of action. Interactions with people yield commitments, which
expand the venture's means and constrain its goals. The cycle repeats until the
emerging artifact, a firm, product, or market, is stable enough to manage
causally (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-ie-effectual-cycle)).

```{r fig-ie-effectual-cycle, fig.cap = "The effectual cycle. Means suggest actions, interactions produce stakeholder commitments, and commitments expand means while converging goals, until a new market or venture takes shape. Adapted from the dynamic model in Sarasvathy (2008)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  M [label = "Means\\n(identity, knowledge,\\nnetworks)", %s]
  G [label = "Possible courses\\nof action", %s]
  I [label = "Interactions with\\npotential stakeholders", %s]
  C [label = "Stakeholder\\ncommitments", %s]
  N [label = "New means and\\nconverging goals", %s]
  O [label = "New venture,\\nproduct, or market", %s]
  U [label = "Uncertainty\\n(unpredictable future)", %s]
  M -> G -> I -> C
  C -> N [label = " expand and\\n constrain"]
  N -> M [label = " cycle", style = dashed, constraint = false]
  N -> O
  U -> I [style = dotted, arrowhead = none]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_construct, node_construct, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

### Evidence and extensions

In a meta-analysis, @read2009 found positive associations between new-venture
performance and several effectual elements, especially the use of existing
means and partnerships, though the evidence was uneven across principles and
many studies relied on cross-sectional, self-reported measures. Effectuation
has become one of the most influential frameworks in entrepreneurship
education, and its emphasis on cheap experiments and stakeholder commitments
overlaps with the practitioner movement known as the **lean startup**.

::: {.debate}
**Is effectuation a theory?** @arend2015 evaluated effectuation against criteria
for theory and concluded that it falls short: its constructs are loosely
defined, its predictions about performance are unclear, and it is hard to
falsify. Proponents responded that effectuation is a theory of expertise and
process, not a performance theory, and that its value lies in describing how
entrepreneurs act under true uncertainty. The exchange is a useful case study
in the criteria discussed in Chapter 2: precision, falsifiability, and scope.
A further issue is causal direction. Experienced entrepreneurs may use
effectual logic because they have succeeded rather than succeed because they
use it.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Lean startups as structured experimentation.** The lean startup method
popularized by @ries2011 and @blank2013 advises founders to treat business
ideas as hypotheses, build a **minimum viable product**, measure customer
responses, and **pivot** or persevere on the basis of what they learn. The
method shares effectuation's distrust of long-range forecasts and its emphasis
on affordable experiments, but it is more causal in spirit: it starts from a
hypothesized customer problem and tests it. Evidence is emerging. In a
randomized field experiment with Italian start-ups, @camuffo2020 found that
founders trained to formulate and test hypotheses scientifically were more
likely to pivot or abandon weak ideas and performed better than a control
group. For managers in established firms, the same logic underlies internal
venture programmes that fund small experiments with stage gates tied to evidence.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The positive relationship between effectual decision making and venture
  survival will be stronger in nascent markets than in established markets.
- *H2.* Ventures that secure pre-commitments from stakeholders before product
  launch will experience fewer and smaller losses on failure.

**Designs.** Think-aloud protocols and decision experiments comparing expert
and novice entrepreneurs, longitudinal panels of nascent ventures, randomized
training interventions.

**Measures.** Validated scales for causation and effectuation, counts of
pre-commitments and partnerships, maximum funds at risk relative to founder
wealth, number of pivots.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Treating effectuation as "no planning".** Effectuation is not improvisation
without discipline. It specifies a logic: bounded downside, stakeholder
commitments, and the deliberate use of surprises. Studies that equate it with
the absence of a business plan measure something else.
:::

## Opportunity Discovery and Creation {#opportunity-discovery-creation}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Entrepreneurship is the study of how opportunities to create
future goods and services are discovered, evaluated, and exploited. Theories
disagree on whether opportunities exist objectively, waiting to be **discovered**
by alert individuals, or are **created** through entrepreneurs' own actions.

**Origins.** Austrian economics and entrepreneurship research. @kirzner1973 on
entrepreneurial alertness. @shane2000 on the individual-opportunity nexus.
@alvarez2007 on discovery versus creation.

**Level of analysis.** Individual entrepreneur and market.

**Key constructs.** Entrepreneurial opportunity, alertness, prior knowledge,
[information asymmetry](#information-asymmetry) (Section \@ref(information-asymmetry)), risk versus uncertainty, enactment.

**Boundary conditions.** Discovery logic fits markets disrupted by exogenous
shocks with knowable outcomes. Creation logic fits settings where no market yet
exists and outcomes cannot be known in advance.

**Related theories.** [Effectuation](#effectuation),
[Information asymmetry](#information-asymmetry) (Section \@ref(information-asymmetry)),
[Creative destruction](#creative-destruction), [Sensemaking](#sensemaking) (Section \@ref(sensemaking)).
:::

### Core logic

@kirzner1973 offered a contrast to Schumpeter. Where Schumpeter's entrepreneur
disrupts equilibrium with new combinations, Kirzner's entrepreneur moves markets
*toward* equilibrium by noticing price discrepancies and unexploited
possibilities that others overlook. The capacity to notice is
**alertness**, and it requires no special resources, only perception.

@shane2000 argued that entrepreneurship research had focused too much on who
entrepreneurs are and too little on opportunities. They defined the field as the
study of the **nexus** between enterprising individuals and valuable
opportunities, and they posed three questions: why, when, and how opportunities
come into existence, why, when, and how some people rather than others discover
and exploit them, and why, when, and how different modes of action are used.
In a companion study, @shane2000a traced eight sets of entrepreneurs who
founded firms to exploit a single MIT three-dimensional printing invention. Each
saw a different application, in markets connected to their prior work, which
suggests that **prior knowledge** shapes which opportunities people discover.

@alvarez2007 sharpened the debate by setting out two internally consistent
theories (Table \@ref(tab:tab-ie-disc-create)).

```{r tab-ie-disc-create}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Assumption, ~`Discovery theory`, ~`Creation theory`,
  "Nature of opportunities", "Exist independently of entrepreneurs, formed by exogenous shocks to markets or technology", "Do not exist until created through entrepreneurs' actions",
  "Nature of entrepreneurs", "Differ from others in alertness or prior knowledge", "May not differ ex ante, differences may emerge through action",
  "Decision context", "Risky: outcomes and their probabilities can be estimated", "Uncertain: outcomes cannot be known in advance",
  "Implied actions", "Search, evaluate, plan, and then exploit", "Act, observe responses, and iterate",
  "Associated approaches", "Kirznerian alertness, information asymmetry", "Effectuation, bricolage, enactment",
  "Philosophical stance", "Critical realism", "Evolutionary realism and social construction"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Discovery versus creation theories of entrepreneurial action (after Alvarez & Barney, 2007).")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The discovery view has generated a large literature on alertness, prior
knowledge, and the cognitive and network sources of opportunity recognition.
The creation view connects to [effectuation](#effectuation), [bricolage](#bricolage),
and sensemaking. Recent work has questioned the opportunity construct itself.
@ramoglou2016 propose that opportunities are best understood as
**propensities**: latent conditions for profitable demand that exist whether or
not anyone acts, but that are only actualized through entrepreneurial action.
This realist position tries to keep the objectivity of discovery while
accommodating the role of action stressed by creation theory.

::: {.debate}
**Can opportunities be observed before they are exploited?** Critics argue that
opportunities are identified only after successful exploitation, so "discovered
opportunity" is often a retrospective label for success. This makes the
construct hard to measure independently of outcomes. A practical response is to
study *beliefs* about opportunities (perceived opportunities) and their
formation, rather than opportunities as such, and to sample ventures that
failed as well as those that succeeded.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: two founders, one technology.** A university develops a
low-cost sensor that detects moisture in materials. One founder, who previously
worked in commercial roofing, sees a leak-detection product for flat roofs. A
second founder, from agriculture, sees a soil-monitoring service for small
farms. The discovery view explains the divergence through prior knowledge, as
in @shane2000a. The creation view would add that each market takes shape only
as the founders persuade early customers, adapt the product, and build
distribution, so the eventual opportunity is partly a product of their actions.
For a technology-transfer office, the implication is to license the same
technology to several founders in different fields rather than search for the
single best application.
:::

## Bricolage {#bricolage}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Resource-constrained entrepreneurs can create value by
**making do** with resources at hand, recombining them for new purposes, and
refusing to accept conventional limits on what those resources can do.

**Origins.** Anthropology and organization theory. @levistrauss1966 introduced
the bricoleur. @baker2005 developed entrepreneurial bricolage from a field study
of resource-constrained firms. @garud2003 applied the idea to technology
development.

**Level of analysis.** Venture and its local resource environment.

**Key constructs.** Resources at hand, making do, recombination, refusal to
enact limitations, parallel versus selective bricolage, domains (physical
inputs, labour, skills, customers, institutional rules).

**Boundary conditions.** Most relevant in resource-scarce environments.
Persistent, wide-ranging bricolage may constrain growth.

**Related theories.** [Effectuation](#effectuation),
[Resource-based theory](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)),
[Combinatorial creativity](#combinatorial-creativity) (Section \@ref(combinatorial-creativity)).
:::

### Core logic

The anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss contrasted the **bricoleur**, who builds
with a heterogeneous stock of materials at hand, with the engineer, who acquires
materials designed for a project [@levistrauss1966]. @baker2005 brought the
concept into entrepreneurship. Their field study of small firms facing severe
resource constraints found that some created something from nothing by treating
undervalued or discarded resources (scrap materials, untrained but willing
workers, ignored customers, ambiguous regulations) as raw material for new
products and services. Resource environments, they argued, are partly
**constructed** by the firms that act in them (Table \@ref(tab:tab-ie-bricolage)).

```{r tab-ie-bricolage}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Domain, ~`What bricolage looks like`, ~Example,
  "Physical inputs", "Using discarded, idle, or unconventional materials", "Repurposing equipment or waste streams from another industry",
  "Labour", "Involving customers, friends, and suppliers as workers", "Customers who help build or test the product",
  "Skills", "Applying amateur or self-taught skills to professional tasks", "A founder writes software without formal training",
  "Customers and markets", "Serving customers that others ignore", "Offering a basic service to buyers who were not served at all",
  "Institutional environment", "Testing ambiguous rules and standards rather than accepting them", "Operating in a gap between regulatory categories"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Domains of entrepreneurial bricolage (organized following Baker & Nelson, 2005).")
```

@baker2005 also distinguished two patterns. **Parallel bricolage**, applied
habitually across many domains at once, tended to trap firms in a small,
idiosyncratic niche, because customers, employees, and products all depended on
improvisation. **Selective bricolage**, confined to a few domains and over a
